reasons: Lake identity matches the title, court, date, docket, and year: Rivas-Villegas v. Cortesluna, U.S. Supreme Court, decided 2021-10-18.
Lake citations list official citation 595 U.S. 1 and parallel citations 142 S. Ct. 4 and 211 L. Ed. 2d 164; vendor_neutral is empty.
The opinion states the issue as whether Rivas-Villegas is entitled to qualified immunity because he did not violate clearly established law.
The opinion applies and refines the clearly-established-law specificity requirement in a Fourth Amendment excessive-force QI setting, supporting the Qualified Immunity home role.
residual_risks: The exact editorial threshold for the word Key is not defined in the disclosed files, but the SCOTUS status and lake progeny/citation metadata support the classification.

defect.evidence_quote:
“[I]n an obvious case, these
standards can ‘clearly establish’ the answer, even without
a body of relevant case law.” Ibid. But this is not an obvi-
ous case. Thus, to show a violation of clearly established
law, Cortesluna must identify a case that put Rivas-Ville-
gas on notice that his specific conduct was unlawful.
defect.problem: The holding states an unconditional QI rule requiring the plaintiff to identify a case. The opinion limits that requirement to this non-obvious case after expressly preserving an obvious-case exception.
defect.proposed_fix: Revise to: In a non-obvious Fourth Amendment excessive-force QI case, the plaintiff must identify precedent that put the officer on notice that his specific conduct was unlawful, because the clearly-established inquiry is undertaken in light of the specific context, not at a high level of generality.

reasons: The quoted 'specific context' language is supported by slip op. 4.
The broader proposition overclaims because the opinion says obvious cases may be clearly established without a body of relevant case law.
residual_risks: The defect is breadth, not the character fidelity of the quoted 'specific context' phrase.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Add the non-obvious-case limitation and avoid stating that every QI plaintiff must identify a case.
